summary: This RFC points out problems in the specification of the Military Standard Internet Protocol (MIL-STD-1777) and proposes solutions, to help people obtain a reliable implementation.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper reads the official military rulebook for IP, finds mistakes, and says how to fix them.

subtitle: A close reading of the Military Standard Internet Protocol reveals six serious implementation bugs.

tldr.problem: The Military Standard Internet Protocol (MIL-STD-1777) is the DoD's official IP specification, written in Ada with formal decision tables. However, a careful analysis reveals several critical bugs that prevent it from working correctly.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents six major problems: the last fragment is not inserted during reassembly, a state transition for ICMP fragments is missing, the reassembly-complete check has incorrect logic, fragment calculations are wrong, the reassembly procedure has implementation errors, and the length given to reassembled datagrams is incorrect. Each problem is explained in detail with proposed corrections.
tldr.outcome: While the RFC does not resolve these issues, it serves as essential guidance for implementors of MIL-STD-1777, warning them of the pitfalls and showing exactly what corrections are needed to produce a working implementation.

today: RFC 963 documents problems with MIL-STD-1777 that were discovered in 1985. The RFC serves as essential documentation for anyone implementing the Military Standard IP, identifying critical bugs and providing corrections needed for a working implementation.

sections.title: Background on MIL-STD-1777
sections.content:
The Military Standard Internet Protocol (MIL-STD-1777, dated August 1983) is the formal DoD standard for IP. Unlike earlier informal specifications, this version was written formally in Ada with decision tables and action procedures, following a rigorous approach to protocol specification.

The RFC is investigating this specification using automatic tools to detect errors. During an initial analysis, the author discovered six major problems and several minor ones. These results come from studying the specification itself, not from testing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The military has an official rulebook for the Internet. Some people are reading it very carefully to check if it has any mistakes before people use it to build systems.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly in IP
sections.content:
A key function of IP is breaking large datagrams into smaller pieces (fragments) to fit through subnetwork links, then reassembling them at the destination. The MIL-STD-1777 specification has particular trouble in this area.

The specification uses a bit map to track which fragments have arrived. Each bit represents an 8-octet block. The most serious problems are: fragmented datagrams are never delivered to the upper layer because the last fragment is not inserted into the reassembled datagram, the reassembly-complete test will always fail, and the length reported for reassembled datagrams is incorrect.
sections.plainLanguage: When pieces of a message arrive, the computer needs to put them back together. The rulebook has mistakes that would make the pieces never get reassembled correctly or delivered.

sections.title: Six Documented Problems
sections.content:
Problem 1: Missing last fragment. A decision table row omits the reassemble action when the last fragment arrives, so incoming fragmented datagrams are delivered with one fragment missing.

Problem 2: Missing state transition. There is no decision table row for the case where an ICMP (control) message arrives fragmented and is complete. This means fragmented ICMP messages are never analyzed.

Problem 3: Errors in reass_done. The function that tests whether reassembly is complete has multiple bugs: it applies the octet-to-block conversion twice, it ignores the fragment offset, and when the tail fragment has arrived, it checks the reassembly map before the incoming fragment is inserted, always returning false.

Problem 4: Fragment size calculation. The procedure that fragments outgoing datagrams fails to ensure each fragment is a multiple of eight octets. As a result, up to seven octets per fragment are never transmitted.

Problem 5: Reassembly procedure errors. The reassembly procedure has range mismatches in array slices that would cause run-time exceptions. For example, one slice copies more bytes than it receives.

Problem 6: Wrong data length. The reassembled-delivery procedure reports the length of only the first fragment to the upper-layer protocol, not the total length of the reassembled datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: The problems are: the last piece doesn't get added, there's no rule for handling control messages in pieces, the test for when reassembly is done has mistakes, pieces are cut at the wrong sizes, the code that puts pieces together would crash, and the wrong length gets reported.

sections.title: Other Implementation Difficulties
sections.content:
Beyond the six major problems, the RFC identifies several difficulties that are not errors per se but are implementation concerns. Padding calculations are done without explicitly accounting for 32-bit alignment required by the spec. Some subnetworks may have maximum transmission sizes smaller than an IP header, making fragmentation impossible; this case is not handled. The specification provides no guidance on how IP should respond to subnetwork errors. Error reporting to upper-layer protocols lacks a field for the datagram identifier, making it hard to correlate errors with original datagrams.

The RFC also notes that Ada syntax errors are scattered throughout the specification: misspelled variable names, incorrect slice assignments, and unnamed record types that are not legal in Ada.
sections.plainLanguage: There are also smaller problems with the rulebook: it forgets about padding, doesn't handle very small networks, and has lots of typos and misspellings.

sections.title: Practical Implications and Solutions
sections.content:
The RFC documents a working C implementation of MIL-STD-1777 that was generated semi-automatically from the specification using a protocol development system. This implementation was possible only after correcting the problems detailed above in the specification itself.

For each problem, the RFC proposes a specific correction: adding the missing reassemble action, inserting the missing decision table row, rewriting the reass_done function logic, adjusting the fragment size calculation, fixing the slice assignments in reassembly, and using the total data length instead of the first fragment's length.

The RFC makes clear that these corrections must be applied before MIL-STD-1777 can serve as a basis for reliable implementations, and anyone implementing this standard should study this document carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors fixed the rulebook mistakes and built a working system. They show exactly what changes need to be made so other people can do the same.
